question: What is the formula for relative frequency?
expected: Relative frequency = frequency / total number of data values, RF = f/n, where f is the frequency of a data value and n is the total number of data values.
with_collection: RF = f/n, where f = frequency and n = total number of data values (or the sum of the individual frequencies).

cited.title: Descriptive Statistics — Histograms, Frequency Polygons, and Time Series Graphs
cited.evidence: $$\text{RF}=\frac{f}{n}$$ with f = frequency, n = total number of data values

note: The formula is stated in the Chapter 2 Histograms section, not in the Chapter 1 Frequency section (which uses relative frequency in tables without stating the formula).

question: A binomial distribution has n = 20 trials and probability of success p = 0.25. What are its mean and standard deviation?
expected: Mean mu = n*p = 20*0.25 = 5. Standard deviation sigma = sqrt(n*p*q) = sqrt(20*0.25*0.75) = sqrt(3.75) = 1.94 (to two decimal places).
with_collection: The mean is mu = np and the standard deviation is sigma = sqrt(npq). Substituting n = 20, p = 0.25, q = 0.75: mu = 5, sigma = sqrt(3.75) = 1.94.

cited.title: Discrete Random Variables — Binomial Distribution
cited.evidence: The mean of X can be calculated using the formula mu = np, and the standard deviation is given by the formula sigma = $\sqrt{npq}$.

note: The pack gives the formulas; the arithmetic (sqrt(3.75) = 1.9365) was computed independently.

question: State the Empirical Rule (the 68-95-99.7 rule) for a normal distribution.
expected: About 68% of the values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two standard deviations, and about 99.7% within three standard deviations.
with_collection: The Empirical Rule: if X has a normal distribution with mean mu and standard deviation sigma, about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two, and about 99.7% within three. It is also known as the 68-95-99.7 rule.

cited.title: The Normal Distribution — The Standard Normal Distribution
cited.evidence: The Empirical Rule ... also known as the 68-95-99.7 rule.

cited.title: Descriptive Statistics — Measures of the Spread of the Data
cited.evidence: This is known as the Empirical Rule.

question: What is the formula for a confidence interval for a single population mean when the population standard deviation is known?
expected: x-bar +/- z_(alpha/2) * (sigma / sqrt(n)): the sample mean plus or minus the z critical value times the standard error sigma/sqrt(n).
with_collection: CI = (x-bar - EBM, x-bar + EBM) where EBM = z * sigma/sqrt(n), the error bound for the mean.

cited.title: Confidence Intervals — A Single Population Mean using the Normal Distribution

question: What is the test statistic for a chi-square test of independence, and what is the null hypothesis?
expected: Test statistic chi-square = sum over all cells of (Observed - Expected)^2 / Expected. Null hypothesis H0: the two variables are independent (there is no association between them).
with_collection: The test statistic sums (O-E)^2/E over all cells (i*j terms of the form (O-E)^2/E). The null hypothesis is that the two factors are independent, e.g. H0: being a cell phone user while driving and receiving a speeding violation are independent events.

cited.title: The Chi-Square Distribution — Test of Independence
cited.evidence: There are i*j terms of the form $\frac{(O-E)^2}{E}$. A test of independence determines whether two factors are independent or not. H0: Being a cell phone user while driving and receiving a speeding violation are independent events.

note: The teaching section ranks 4th in the FTS5 top hits for the query (behind the Facts and Comparison sections); the formula and H0 are verified in the section text itself.
